issues.item: Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed
issues.explanation: 'Feeling happy or relaxed' as a trigger is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only broad internal-state trigger alongside trauma-linked cues (hearing related names, ambulances) and is weakly connected to the rest of the formulation. The other nodes emphasize intrusive war memories, negative self-appraisals, and avoidance; a relaxation trigger without any corresponding threat content or appraisals about letting guard down is clinically hard to anchor here.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Mirror Checking: keep checking mirrors
issues.explanation: 'Keep checking mirrors' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile. Mirror checking usually implies appearance/body-focused concern or hypervigilant scanning for current danger, but this profile has no Threat items and the formulation isolates Threat from the active network. The remaining maladaptive strategies (avoiding sleep, revenge fantasies) fit trauma intrusions and appraisals, whereas mirror checking addresses a symptom theme not otherwise represented.

vignette: Seventy-two years ago, while working the late shift at a supply depot near the forward perimeter, Duy had been stacking crates when the first shell struck the earth nearby. The ground heaved, dirt and splintered timber filled the air, and a deafening roar swallowed the courtyard. He did not hear the others call his name at first; he only felt the violent impact of the blast and the sudden, disorienting silence that followed. Even now, in his seventh decade, Duy remains certain that another man would have taken cover or simply lain still. He had always believed he ought to have done more, that his own hesitation had left him exposed in a way others had not been. Years later, the memories of that morning refused to settle into the quiet archive of old age. They arrived without warning, vivid and detailed, the smoke and cracked earth so clear that Duy sometimes caught himself bracing against a sky that was perfectly blue. What frightened him most was how often these recollections forced their way into his thoughts when he was trying to eat his morning coffee or listen to his wife speak. The memories felt less like his own experiences and more like footage playing out through someone else's eyes. He had come to believe that if he tried to name what had happened, the weight would crush him, so he kept his mind carefully turned away from the event. Now working his final years as a firefighter, Duy spent his shifts in the station bay, a concrete space that routinely stirred the old alarms. When an ambulance wailed past the station gates, the siren did not sound like routine emergency care; it sounded like a warning. A dropped toolbox or a neighbor's backfiring truck could provoke the same sharp turn of his head. When his wife called his given name, or when a dispatch officer repeated the syllables of his callsign, the sound alone pulled him forward into the courtyard of his mind. He checked the environment constantly, eyes tracing the fence line, the driveway, the horizon, looking for signs that the ground might heave again. His wife had grown accustomed to his vigilance, though she noted how he would sometimes stare at his own hands as if they belonged to a stranger, caught in the quiet certainty that he was less a man than a tool waiting for a command. Alongside the vigilance, Duy developed habits that simply occupied his days. He avoided lying down before dusk, preferring to sit in the armchair with the lamp on, convinced that darkness would let the old scenes rise unchecked. When sleep finally took him, his revenge fantasies often played out in the dim hours. He would watch the ceiling, imagining himself returning to the supply depot, confronting the unseen hands that had let the supply lines falter, setting everything straight in the quiet theater of his mind. These thoughts did not feel like worries; they felt like duties waiting to be fulfilled. The memories remained bright, the avoidance of thought a shield he never quite lowered, and the sense that he was an object among people never quite dissolved. Recently, a particularly loud bang from a passing delivery truck sent him searching the living room for a threat that was no longer there. Standing there, heart steady but mind still tracing the old perimeter, Duy realized he was ready to speak. He had come to seek help not because the fear was too great, but because he hoped to find a way to let the memories belong to him, and to stop waiting for the next sky to crack.
